{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Elizabeth Buchanan Cowley''' (1874–1945) was an American mathematician.

==Life==
Cowley was born on May 22, 1874, in [[Allegheny, Pennsylvania]].<ref name="asc">{{citation|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/cowley.htm|title=Elizabeth Buchanan Cowley|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|first=Larry|last=Riddle|publisher=[[Agnes Scott College]]|date=January 10, 2014|accessdate=2015-10-08|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304113758/https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/cowley.htm|url-status=live}}.</ref><ref>[[:File:Woman s Who s who of America.pdf]], 1914, p. 210 (= p. 199 in Pdf)</ref> She had four siblings, but they and her father all died by 1900.<ref name="gl"/> Cowley's mother, Mary Junkin Buchanan Cowley, later became a member of the Board of Public Education of [[Pittsburgh]], and was the namesake of the Mary J. Cowley School in Pittsburgh. Cowley's grandfather (Mary Cowley's father) was James Galloway Buchanan, a surgeon in the [[Union Army]].<ref name="thornton">{{citation|title=History of Pittsburgh and Environs, from Prehistoric Days to the Beginning of the American Revolution|volume=4|first=George Thornton|last=Fleming|publisher=American Historical Society, Incorporated|year=1922|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1M8wAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA107|pages=107–108}}.</ref>

Cowley earned a bachelor's degree in 1893 from the [[Indiana University of Pennsylvania|Indiana State Normal School of Pennsylvania]], and became a school teacher. She earned a second bachelor's degree in 1901 and a master's degree in 1902 from [[Vassar College]], and became an instructor at Vassar, studying higher mathematics during the summers at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="asc"/><ref name="gl"/> In 1908 she completed a doctorate from [[Columbia University]]. Her dissertation, on [[algebraic curve]]s, was supervised by [[Cassius Jackson Keyser]]; she became the fourth woman to earn a doctorate in mathematics from Columbia.<ref name="asc"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=38626}}</ref> Continuing to work at Vassar, Cowley was promoted to assistant professor in 1913, and associate professor in 1916. She went on leave in 1926 to assist her mother, and resigned her position at Vassar in 1929, instead becoming a high school teacher in Pittsburgh.<ref name="asc"/><ref name="gl"/>

She retired from teaching in 1938, had a stroke in 1941, and died on April 13, 1945, in [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida]].<ref name="gl">{{citation|title=Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD's|volume=34|series=History of mathematics|first1=Judy|last1=Green|author1-link=Judy Green (mathematician)|first2=Jeanne|last2=LaDuke|author2-link=Jeanne LaDuke|publisher=American Mathematical Society|year=2009|isbn=9780821843765|title-link=Pioneering Women in American Mathematics|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IRbOAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA163|pages=163–164|contribution=Cowley, Elizabeth B.}} Biography on p.148-152 of the
[https://www.ams.org/bookpages/hmath-34-PioneeringWomen.pdf Supplementary Material] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107165628/https://www.ams.org/bookpages/hmath-34-PioneeringWomen.pdf |date=2017-11-07 }} at [https://www.ams.org/publications/authors/books/postpub/hmath-34 AMS] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190327172504/https://books.google.de/books?id=IRbOAwAAQBAJ |date=2019-03-27 }}</ref>

==Contributions==
Cowley and her co-author Ida Whiteside won a prize for a 1907 paper they wrote on the orbit of comet C/1825 V1. Another of her publications, in 1926, concerned [[liquid water pouring puzzles]]. She was the author of two textbooks on plane and solid geometry, published in 1932 and 1934, and advocated teaching solid geometry to high school students after many colleges had replaced the subject with freshman calculus.<ref name="asc"/> She published another book in 1941 about public education.<ref name="gl"/>

==Associations==
Cowley was an early member of the [[Mathematical Association of America]], and became a member of its board of trustees when it incorporated in 1920.
She was an [[list of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers|invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1932, speaking there about [[mathematics education]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php|title=ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers since 1897|publisher=[[International Mathematical Union]]|accessdate=2015-10-01|archive-date=2017-11-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171124141541/http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php|url-status=dead}}.</ref> She also belonged to the [[American Mathematical Society]], [[German Mathematical Society]], and [[Circolo Matematico di Palermo]].<ref name="thornton"/>
